lawyer:
Md Khalilur Rahman with Md Rashidul Karim and Junaed Hossen Khan, Advocates—For the Plaintiff-Appellant. 
Probir Neogi, Senior Advocate with Mohammad Jamal Hossain, Advocates—For the Defendants-Respondents No. 1-2. 
AM Masum with Md Farhad Bin Hossain, Advocates—For the Defendants-Respondents No. 3.
parties:
Amin Md Lands Development Limited......Plaintiff-Appellant
vs
Monira Munni and others……….Contesting-Defendants-Respondents
full_judgment:
AKM Abdul Hakim J : This appeal at the instance of the plaintiff is directed against the judgment and decree dated 22-2-2018 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Seventh Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 54 of 2016 dismissing the suit for Specific Performance of contract.

2. Facts necessary for disposal of the appeal briefly, be put thus: Plaintiff Company Amin Mohammad Lands Development Limited instituted Title Suit No. 110 of 2009 for Specific Performance of Contract on 22-2-2009 in the Second Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka impleading respondent Nos. 1 and 2 as defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and respondent No. 3 as pro-forma defendant No. 3 which was subsequently transferred to the Court of Joint District Judge, Seventh Court, Dhaka and renumbered as Title Suit No. 54 of 2016 alleging, inter alia, that the defendant No. 1 acquired the land measuring 2.85 acres as described in schedule 'ka' to the plaint was purchased by the defendant No. 1 by registered kabala No. 17274 dated 30-6-2005 from Adnan Co-operative Housing Society Ltd; that defendant No. 1 also purchased the land measuring 0.6264 Ajutansha described in schedule 'kha' to the plaint by way of registered kabala No. 16729 dated 30-6-2005 from Abdul Matin and Md Nazrul Islam; that while possessing the suit land comprising schedules 'ka' and `kha' to the plaint measuring total area of 3.4764 mortgaged the schedule land to defendant No. 3-Bank against the loan Case No. BASIC /DIL/CREDIT/2008/247 obtained by defendant No. 2, husband of the defendant No. 1 as security of the aforesaid loan; that at this stage, defendant No. 1 through her husband, defendant No. 2 offered to transfer the suit land to the plaintiff to redeem the schedule 'ka' and 'kha' suit land at a total consideration of Taka 3,07,31,200 whereupon the plaintiff company agreed to purchase the same, and accordingly, executed a registered "Bainanama Dalil" (বায়নানাম দলিল) on 10-4-2008 in respect of the suit land fixing the total value of the land Taka 1,15,00,000 out of which Taka 40,00,000 was paid by the plaintiff's company as earnest money through cheque No. 139325 of HSBC Bank; that on the same day (10-4-2008) another (চুক্তিপত্র) Deed of Agreement was executed between the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 and 2 for redeeming of the suit land which was mortgaged to the defendant No. 3-Bank; that in the said agreement total consideration was fixed Taka 1,92,31,200 for redeeming the mortgage land from the Bank and out which a sum of Taka 5,00,000 was paid in advance on 18-3-2008 and Taka 20,00,000 on 2-4-2008 in cash and at the time of agreement on 10-4-2008 paid a further sum of Taka 85,00,000 by cheque No. 1393256 dated 10-4-2008. Accordingly, the defendant No. 1 received total amount of Taka 1,50,00,000 against Bainanama and Deed of Agreement and on the same day delivered possession of the suit land to the plaintiff company; that after taking delivery of possession of the suit 'ka' and 'kha' schedule land defendant No. 1 further received Taka 5,00,000 on 29-5-2008 by signing a voucher and assured that she will redeem the suit land from the Bank within 15-10-2008. It was further stated that although the defendant No. 1 received total amount of Taka 1,55,00,000 but did not take steps to redeem the suit land from the bank as per bainanama and Deed of Agreement; that later on the plaintiff company enquired in the office of defendant No. 3-Bank and came to learn that the defendant No. 1 deposited only Taka 70,00,000 in the loan account against receipt of Taka 1,55,00,000 from the plaintiff company for re-payment of the loan of the defendant No. 3-Bank; that since the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 did not take step to pay the loan of the Bank, plaintiff-company sent a notice to the defendants and requested them to receive the balance amount after paying off the entire loan-liabilities and execute the sale deed in favour of the plaintiff-company; that after receipt of said letter, defendant No. 2 met with the Director of the plaintiff's company and again assured to execute and register sale deed after redeeming the mortgage; that while the plaintiff's company possessing the suit 'ka' and 'kha' schedule land by constructing boundary wall and also constructed one semi-pucca two roomed house inside the 'ka' schedule land and using the said house as site office and guard room of the "Ashulia Abakash No. 2" project; that on 08-2-2009 the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 sent a letter informing that since the defendants required more money than the money paid by the plaintiff's company to redeem their mortgaged land and due to non-payment of more money, they could not redeem their mortgaged land, moreover, the period of bainanama was already expired in the meantime, they are no more bound by the agreement and as such they requested the plaintiff company to execute "Bainapatra Return Deed" /"Deed of Recession of Bainapatra"; that the plaintiff company asked the defendant No. 1 to complete the transaction on receipt of the balance consideration but this was of no avail. On these allegations, the plaintiff brought the suit for Specific Performance of contract with a prayer for paying the loan of defendant No. 3-Bank after redeeming the mortgage of the suit land mortgaged with Bank from the deposited amount of Taka 1,52,31,200 deposited under Bangladesh Bank challan No. 10233 dated 24-2-2009 and execute the necessary sale deed in respect of schedule 'ka' and 'kha of the suit land after receiving the balance consideration money. In case of default by the defendant No. 1 and 2 in executing and registering the necessary sale deed in favour of the plaintiff company, directed the defendant No. 3-Bank to redeem the mortgaged property after receiving its loan money from the deposited amount of Taka 1,52,31,200 deposited in court at the time of filing of suit on 24-2-2009.

3. The suit was contested by defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and defendant No. 3 by filing separate written Statements. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 filed written statement on 15-10-2009 and made a general denial of the averments made in the plaint. The positive case of defendant No. 1 and 2 are that they admitted the Bainanama Dalil (shortly Baina) and Deed of Agreement both dated 10-4-2008 in respect of suit land as alleged in the plaint. But they contended that the suit land was mortgaged to a Bank. It is further stated that as per terms of the Baina, the defendants will pay the banks liabilities within two months from the Baina dated 10-4-2008 and submitted the documents to the plaintiff-company. Although defendants tried their label best to redeem the mortgaged schedule property but due to increased of the loan amount they could not redeem the land. In spite of repeated oral requests made by the defendants to pay the balance money in order to redeem the mortgage land from the bank but the plaintiff did not take any steps to pay the balance money rather the plaintiff by concealing the real facts sent a notice on 24-12-2008. In this state of affairs the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 sent a notice to the plaintiff on 8-2-2009 intimating that the plaintiff had failed to perform his part of the agreement which was executed to repay the loan liabilities and requested to take back the earnest money. As the 2(two) months time as stipulated in Baina has expired, the defendants rescinded the Baina since the time being the essence of the contract and as such the contract is no more enforceable. They further contended that as per Deed of Agreement, since the plaintiff have alternative remedy, the present suit is not maintainable and the plaintiff have/had no remedy as per Transfer of Property Act. With these averments, the defendants prayed for dismissal of the suit.

4. The proforma defendant No. 3, Basic Bank Ltd. contested the suit by filing written statement on 15-10-2009. The case of the defendant No. 3 is that the defendant Bank, has allowed an Over Draft facility in favour of its client namely Bushra Associate (hereinafter referred as the borrower) for an amount of Taka 22.00 lac (twenty two lac) vide its sanction letter No.BASIC/DIL/CREDIT/2005 /3107 Dated 27-8-2005, subsequently the said loan facility was rescheduled and enhanced on several occasions. It is pertinent to mention here that as security of the said Over Draft facility Mrs Munira Munni i.e., the defendant No. 1 of the instant suit has mortgaged her landed property (more specifically mentioned in the schedule-B) vide Registered Mortgage Deed being No. 20083 dated 31-8-2005 in favour of the defendant Bank and she also executed a Registered Power of Attorney being No. 20084 dated 31-8-2005 empowering the defendant Rank to sell the Mortgaged Property. That after availing the said loan facility the borrower failed to repay loan amount to defendant Bank. The defendant Bank has issued several reminder and request letters to the borrower to repay the loan liabilities but no effect as a result the total liability stands at Taka 2,35,51,987.20 as on 31-12-2009 including upto date interest accrued thereon. That it is also mentionable here that one Mr Khandaker Mehmood Alam Nadim has availed an Over Draft facility which now stands at Taka 68,26,000 only as 31-12-2009 where the defendant No. 1 of the suit has also executed letter of Guarantee in favour of the defendant Bank as security of the loan facility extended to said Khandaker Mehmood Alam Nadim. That it is further stated the plaintiff having knowledge regarding mortgage of the suit property and as well as the legal consequence of a mortgage formalities with a malafide intention inpleaded the instant defendant Bank as proforma-defendant No. 3 as such, the plaintiff has never entitle to get any relief against the instant defendant Bank. That it is humbly submitted that the defendant Bank has no knowledge regarding the alleged Bainanama and the defendant Bank has absolute interest upon the properties which is mortgaged to the Bank till adjustment of the loan liabilities or till the date when the defendant Bank execute a Deed of Redemption.

5. On the pleadings, the trial court framed the following issues in the suit.

১। মোকদ্দমাটি তামাদিতে বারিত কিনা?

২। মোকদ্দমাটি বর্তমান আকারে ও প্রকারে চলতে পারে কিনা?

৩। বাদীপক্ষ চুক্তি প্রবলের ডিক্রী পেতে পারে কিনা?

৪ । বাদীপক্ষ প্রা্র্থীত মতে প্রতিকার পেতে পারে কিনা?

6. In the suit plaintiff examined as many as 3 witnesses, and exhibited some documents

which was marked as Exhibits No. 1-5(1). On the contrary, the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 examined 2 (two) dw's to prove their case and filed documents marked as Exhibit KA-KA(3). In support of the written statement filed by the defendant No. 3, they neither filed any documents nor adduced any witness to prove its case.

7. The learned Joint District Judge having heard respective parties and considered the evidence adduced by the parties dismissed the suit against the defendants by the impugned judgment and decree dated 22-2-2018 on the findings that admittedly the suit land was mortgaged to the defendant No. 3-Bank. But before executing the Bainanama defendants did not obtain permission from the defendant -Bank and defendant Bank is not a party in the Baina and Deed of Agreement as such the disputed Bainanama (Exhibit-2) is not a Bainanama in the eye of law and same is barred under provision of section 53D of the Transfer of Property Act. Thus the plaintiff is not entitled to get decree for Specific Performance of Contract as per Bainanama Dali I (Exhibit-2).

8. That being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree dated 22-2-2018, the plaintiff has preferred the present appeal.

9. Mr Md Khalilur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant submits that as per terms of the Bainanama the sale deed would be executed and registered by the defendant No. 1 on payment of loan amount and after redeeming the suit mortgage land which was mortgaged to the defendant-Bank. In elaborating his submission, the Learned Advocate argues that in a contract where on either side there are promises to be performed and the promises are so connected to each other, performance of one is dependent on another, it is said to be condition precedent to the right of action on the reciprocal promise. Learned Advocate further submits that in the present suit mortgagee-Bank-defendant No. 3 was impleaded and requested to withdrew the loan amount from the deposited balance Taka 1,52,31,000 filed by challan dated 24-2-2009 on the date of filing of the suit on 24-2-2009. But the Bank without withdrawing the arrear loan amount from the said deposit of Taka 1,52,31,000 filed written statement stating that for non-payment/default of the defendant No. 2 the over draft loan of Taka 22,00,000 same was enhanced to Taka 2,35,51,987.20 as on 31-12-2009 and further stated another over draft loan of defendant No. 2, which has now stood Taka 68,26,000 as on 31-12-2009. So, the Bank is now entitled (Taka 2,35,51,987.20 + 68,26,000) = Total Taka 3,03,77,987.20 with interest till the mortgage is redeemed in future. Learned Advocate by referring section 47 of Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 next submits that the Bank in no circumstances claims more than 3 times against the principal loan i.e. Taka 22,00,000 x 3 = Taka 66,00,000 which can be easily adjustable from the deposit amount of Taka 1,52,31,000 remaining balance amount of Taka 86,31,200. On the other hand, another Over Draft loan now stood at Taka 68,26,000 with interest as on 31-12-2009 can also be adjusted from the balance deposited amount Taka 86,31,200. So, the Mortgage-Bank is in no way would be prejudiced. He also submits that since the Bank had not filed any suit claiming the loan amount, the same is barred under section 46 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003. Thus the court can easily decreed the present suit for Specific Performance of Contract as per prayer made in the suit directing the defendant No. 3-Mortgagee Bank to redeem the mortgage after receiving its due arrear of loan from the balance deposit amount of Taka 1,52,31,000 deposited in court on 24-2-2009 at the time of filing of the present suit.

10. Learned Advocate for the plaintiff further submits that as per clause 3 of the Bainanama, the defendants delivered the suit land to the plaintiff company and under section 91 of the Evidence Act no evidence can be adduced against the terms of contract. Apart from the above point of law it appears from the agreement that the nature of the property described in agreement was vacant land. But from the oral evidences of the parties and also from the written statement of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 it is found that the suit land is now consists of semi pucca structure surrounded by pucca boundary wall and being used as city office of the Housing Project named "Ashulia Abakash-2", which clearly evident that whatever improvement has been made on the vacant land after execution of Bainanama Dalil dated 10-4-2008 (Exhibit-2). He lastly submits that the learned Joint District Judge mis-conceived the provisions of section 53D of the Transfer of Property Act and failed to consider that Bainanama Dalil or Deed of Agreement for Sale is not barred under the amended provision of section 53D of the Transfer of Property Act as the "Bainanama Dalil" or "Agreement for Sale" is not a "Deed of Transfer" or "Deed of Sale" as such, has committed gross illegality in not passing the decree for specific performance for the suit land. In support of his contentions learned Advocate referred the decisions reported in 44 DLR (AD) 83, 34 DLR (AD) 42, 7 BLD 202, 65 DLR (AD) 130, 57 DLR (AD) 38 and 8 DLR 629.

11. Mr Probir Neogi, learned Advocate for the defendant Nos. land 2-respondents, in upholding the impugned judgment and decree has submitted that the trial court was absolutely right in refusing the specific performance in view of the fact that admittedly the suit property was under mortgage before executing the alleged Baina and Deed of Agreement with Basic Bank Ltd. defendant No. 3 and therefore the alleged Baina and Agreement are void as per section 53D of the Transfer of Property Act. The intention of this provision to secure the public money lies with the Bank and therefore this provisions includes the Agreement for sale within the meaning of “Sold” as provided under section 53D of the Transfer of Property Act since there is a decree in respect of the suit mortgage property. In this connection Mr Neogi has referred to the decision reported in 53 DLR 535. Learned Advocate further submits that in the present case, the plaintiff has alternative remedy by way of receiving compensation in the form of money in case of breach, the contract cannot be specifically enforced. On this point he has referred a decision reported in AIR 1943 (Calcutta) 586. He next submits that the plaintiff failed to performs his part of the agreement within 6 (six) months as stipulated in the amended section 54A of the Transfer of Property Act. In the present case, the Baina was executed on 10-4-2008 and same was valid till 10-10-2008 but the plaintiff did not take any step for registration as per terms of the contract within 6 months. In this respect he has cited decisions reported in 26 BLT (AD) 11, 32 BLD 326 and 5 BLD (AD) 51. He finally submits that plaintiff filed the suit for Specific Performance of Contract in pursuance of two agreements, one registered “Bainanama Dalil” dated 10-4-2008 (Exhibit-2) and another unregistered. “চুক্তিপত্র দলিল”dated 10-4-2008 (Exhibit- 3) and also by depositing balance amount Taka 1,52,31,200 in pursuance of unregistered agreement which indicates that the plaintiff filed the suit by unregistered agreement. Thus the suit is barred under section 54A of the Transfer of Property Act, 17A of the Registration Act and section 21A of the Specific Relief Act, since one of two agreements for sale by which the plaintiff sought specific performance of contract is unregistered.

12. AM Masum, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the defendant No.3 Basic Bank Limited by endorsing the legal submission made by the learned Advocate for the defendant Nos. 1 and 2, submits that the plaintiff is not entitled to get relief in this suit. In support of his submission he cited two decisions reported in 57 DLR (AD) 64 and 63 DLR (AD) 326. He further argued that the present suit is barred under section 22 of the Specific Relief Act and on this point referred the decision of 53 DLR 535. Mr Masum by referring section 20 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain 2003 strenuously argued that no suit can be filed in any court challenging the decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat.

13. Heard the learned Advocate of the respective parties at length, perused the oral and documentary evidence, relevant provision of Specific Relief Act, Registration Act, Evidence Act, Artha Rin Adalat Ain, Contract Act, Limitation Act and the decisions referred by the learned Advocate of the respective parties.

14. It appears that the registered Bainanama Deed dated 10-4-2008 (Exhibit- 2) on which the plaintiff have based its claim in the present suit for Specific Performance of Contract. Admittedly, the defendant No. 1 is the executant of this Baina Deed. By this Bainanama, its executant, defendant No. 1 stipulated to sell to the plaintiff the suit schedules ‘ka’ and ‘kha’ land having an total area of 3.4764 acres fixing total price of the land at Taka 1,15,00,000. It was further stipulated in the Baina amongst others that defendant No. 1 received Taka 40,00,000 from the plaintiff as earnest money and agreed to execute necessary sale Deed /Deeds in favour of the plaintiff or its nominee and get it registered within 6 months from the date of the Bainanama Deed and balance consideration Taka 75,00,000 will be paid at the time of registration of the sale Deed. On the date of Bainanama, defendant No. 1 also delivered khas possession of the suit land. In the Bainanama it was further agreed that since the suit land was mortgaged to the defendant No. 3-Basic Bank Ltd., the defendant No.1 and 2 jointly execute a deed of agreement dated 10-4-2008 (Exhibit- 3) and in the said agreement it was stipulated that defendant No. 1 and her husband defendant No. 2 will redeem the mortgaged property by paying loan liability together with interest from their own source and at their responsibility within a period of 2 (two) months and furnished the original title deeds to the plaintiff-company. It is also stipulated that if the defendants fail and/or neglect to execute and register the Sale Deeds, the plaintiff will be entitled to obtain the deed through the process of the court.

15. It further appears that a Deed of Agreement dated 10-4-2008 (Exhibit-3) was executed between the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 2. In clause 5 of the said agreement, it was stipulated that the suit land was mortgaged to the defendant No. 3-Bank against the Bank loan in Loan Case No. BASIC/DIL/CREDIT/2005 /78 and Bank loan Case No. BASIC/DIL/CREDIT/2006/1035 and the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 will redeem the suit land after paying the entire loan liabilities including interest within a period of two months and submits the original title deed to the plaintiff company.

16. It also appears that the Bainanama Dalil and Deed of Agreement both dated 10-4-2008 (Exhibit-2 and 3) are admitted by both the parties. The defendant No. 3-Bank in its written statement dated 15-10-2009 also admitted that schedule 'ka' and 'kha' of the suit land was mortgaged by the defendant No. 1 against the loan taken by the husband of defendant No. 2. The plaintiff in paragraph No.7 of the plaint clearly stated that that defendant No.1 mortgaged the suit land in defendant No.3 Basic Bank Limited against the Loan Case No. BASIC /DIL/CREDIT/2008/2427 as security of the said loan. In reply to the paragraph No.7 of the plaint, defendant No. 3 in paragraph No.17 of the written statement stated that those are matters of record and as such the defendants are refrained from making any comments. In paragraph No. 26(b) of the written statement it was categorically stated that an amount of Taka 22.00 lac (twenty two lac) was sanctioned to defendant No. 2 vide its sanction letter No. BASIC/DIL/CREDIT/2005/3107 DATED 27-8-2005, subsequently the said loan facility was rescheduled and enhanced on several occasions. It is pertinent to mention here that as security of the said over draft facility defendant No. 1 of the instant suit has mortgaged her landed property vide registered mortgage deed being No. 20083 dated 31-8-2005 in favour of the defendant Bank and defendant No.1 also executed a registered power of attorney being No. 20084 dated 31-8-2005 empowering the defendant bank to sell the mortgaged property; that after availing the said loan facility the borrower failed to repay loan amount, defendant bank issued several reminders and request letters to the borrower to repay the loan liabilities but no effect, as a result the total liability stands at Taka 2,35,51,987.20 as on 31-12-2009 including upto date interest accrued thereon; that it is also mentionable here that defendant No.2 availed an over draft facility which now stands at Taka 68,26,000 on 31-12-2009 where the defendant No. 1 of the suit has also executed letter of guarantee in favour of the defendant bank as security of the loan facility extended to the said defendant No. 2.

17. From the facts and circumstances and evidence on record it appears that defendant No. 3 although contested the suit by filing written statement but did not adduce any oral or documentary evidence to prove that a sum of total Taka 3,03,77,987.20 was remained outstanding against the loan accounts of defendant No. 2 and defendant No. 3 in its written statement did not disclose that for realisation of outstanding loan bank filed Artha Rin suit and obtained decree for realization of aforesaid loan amount against the defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 2 and also in respect of suit land. The defendant No. 3 has absolute interest upon the properties which is mortgaged to the Bank till adjustment of the loan liabilities or till date when the defendant-Bank execute a Deed of Redemption.

18. The issues that falls for determination in this appeal whether the parties have intended to conclude the transaction with the stipulated time of six months and secondly, whether the plaintiff has failed to perform his promise which compelled to the defendants to rescind the Bainanama, Thirdly, whether the plaintiff has failed to perform its promise which compelled the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 to rescind the Bainanama Dalil and finally, whether the Bainanaman Dalil and Deed of Agreement (Exhibit-2 and 3) are barred under section 53D of the Transfer of Property Act.

19. The defendant No. 1 admit the execution of Bainanama Dalil and Deed of Agreement and receiving payment of advance money Taka 1,57,31,200 out of total consideration Taka 3,07,31,200 and did not dispute that suit land was mortgaged to defendant No. 3-Bank against loan taken by defendant No. 2. But defendant Nos. 1 and 2 on the other hand, disputes the delivery of possession of the suit land at the time of execution of Bainanama Dalil. In view of the conflicting claims, the determination of the issues in controversy depends on the construction of the Bainanama Dalil (Exhibit- 2) and Deed of Agreement (Exhibit-3) executed by the parties. After execution of Baina, later on 29-5-2008, defendant No. 1 further received a sum of Taka 5,00,000 remaining total balance consideration amount Taka 1,52,31,200 at the time of filing of suit.

20. On the close reading of the Bainanama Dalil (Exhibit-2) there is no gain saying that there is obligation on the part of the defendant No. 1 to comply with the conditions stipulated in the Baina. Though there is an stipulation to complete the transaction within a period of 6(six) months, this time limit was circumscribed by the fulfillment of the obligation by the defendant No. 1, who was not given unconditional power to rescind the Baina for non-payment of the balance consideration within 6(six) months. The defendant No. 1 is under obligation to deliver documents of title and other paper after redeeming the mortgage of the suit land and paying the outstanding loan amount of defendant No. 3-Bank. After completing the aforesaid obligations, then the Sale Deed /Deeds will be executed and registered on payment of balance consideration of money Taka 1,52,31,200.

21. Unless the defendant No. 1 performs her part of obligation, the plaintiff will not be able to get the registered Sale Deed and clear title of the suit land. The mortgaged property shall be redeemed first for purpose of completion of the transaction. The defendant No. 1 without contacting the plaintiff for completing the transaction for redeeming the mortgage of the suit land unilaterally rescinded the Baina on 8-2-2009. There is nothing on the record that the defendant No. 1 has intimated the plaintiff she has adjusted the loan and redeem the suit land from defendant No.3 Bank and there is no impediment for executing Sale Deed and she is ready and willing to execute the Sale Deed.

22. In a contract where on either side there are promises to be performed and the promises are so related to each other, performance of one is dependent on another, it is said to be condition precedent to the right of action on the reciprocal promise. The ordinary rule governing vendors and purchasers is that the payment of the consideration is to be simultaneous with the execution of the deed and shall be made at the time when the deed is executed by the vendor. Contracts are normally made up of various statements and promise on both sides, differing in character and importance; the parties may regard some of these as vital, others as subsidiary, or collateral to the main purpose of the contract. Where one of these is broken, the traditional approach of the court has been to discover, from the tenor of the contract or the expressed intention of the parties, whether the broken was vital to the contract or not. If the parties regarded the term as essential, it is a condition; its failure entitles the innocent party to treat himself as discharged from liability. In law in contracts consisting of reciprocal promises, the promises on either side are considerations for one another. In bilateral contracts, the parties not only exchange promises but also bargain for an exchange of the promised performances.

23. Section 51 of the Contract Act enacts that when a contract consists of reciprocal promises to be simultaneously performed, no promisor need perform his promise unless the promisee is ready and willing to perform his reciprocal promise. Whether there are reciprocal promises to be simultaneously performed, no promisee need perform his promise unless the promisor is ready and willing to perform his reciprocal promise. While section 52 of the said Act makes provision for contracts in which order reciprocal promises are to be performed is expressly fixed by the contract and, in which case, the reciprocal promises are to be performed in that order; and where the order is not expressly fixed by the contract, the reciprocal promises are to be performed in that order which the nature of the transaction requires. Section 53 provides that when a contract contains reciprocal promises and one party to the contract prevents the order from performing his promise, the contract becomes voidable at the option of the party so prevented. Section 54 completes the cases where on either side, there is promise to be performed, but the promises are so related to each other, or to one another, that the performance on one side is a condition precedent to a claim for performance on the other. The essential elements of this section are; (a) the contract must consist of reciprocal promises; (b) the reciprocal promises must be such that (i) one of them cannot be performed; or (ii) its performance cannot be claimed, till the other has been performed; and (iii) the promisor of the promise last mentioned fails to perform it.

24. In a contract containing reciprocal promises, if one party fails to perform his part of obligation thereby he/she prevents the other party performing his/her promise and in such eventuality the contract becomes voidable at the option of the party so prevented and the party so prevented is entitled to compensation from the other party for any loss which he may sustain in consequence of non-performance of the contract. The reason is that one who prevents a thing from being done is not allowed to avail himself of the non-performance which he himself has occasioned, since it is his own act which has brought about that result, and, therefore, he cannot complain that he is damnified. No one can be permitted to find a claim upon his own inequity or to take advantage of his own wrong. Prevention by one party to fulfill the promise is tantamount to a fulfillment of the promise by the party prevented in a case of conditional contract or a contract containing reciprocal promises.

25. If a promisor is himself the cause of the failure of performance, either of an obligation due to him or of a condition upon which his own liability depends, he cannot take advantage of such failure. The principle that prevention by one party excuses performance by the other, both of a condition and of a promise holds good broadly in all cases. The condition of promise is excused, because the promisor has caused non-performance. Where a party stipulates that another shall do a certain things, he thereby impliedly promises that he will himself do nothing which will hinder or obstruct that other in doing that thing. If the situation is such, that the co-operation of one party is an essential prerequisite to performance by the other, there is not only a condition implied in fact qualifying the promise of the latter, but also an implied promise by the former to give the necessary co-operation. In the present case, the defendant No. 1 completely ignored her promises but only stressed upon the non-payment of the balance consideration by the plaintiff. But the trial court totally failed to consider this vital aspect of the case and erred in law in dismissing the suit for specific performance.

26. There is no dispute that a time limit has been mentioned in the agreement for payment of the balance consideration which should not be considered in isolation and if the agreement as a whole is considered there will be any doubt that this time limit is secondary in nature in view of the fact that this time limit is dependent upon certain facts. The defendant is under obligation to perform his part of the promise first and there is nothing on record to assume that she has performed his part of the promise. The performance of the promise of the plaintiff depended upon the performance of the defendants promise.

27. In contracts for sale of immovable property, the fact that a specific time is fixed for payment or for conveyance does not normally make time of the essence. Failure to pay at a fixed time is not per se sufficient to terminate the seller's duty to convey; and failure to convey on the exact date does not per se discharged the buyer. In such agreements, usually time is not be essence of contract the reason being that the law of equity which governs rights of the parties in cases of specific performance of contracts of sale of immovable property, looks not at the letter but at the substance of the agreement. The intention to treat time as the essence of the contract may be evidenced by circumstances which are sufficiently strong to displace the normal presumption that in a contract for sale of real estate, stipulation as to time is not the essence of the contract.

28. Now turning to the facts of the present case, the agreement that is Bainanama Dalil in question was executed on 10-4-2008 and though there was stipulation for completing the transaction within six months it was obligatory on the part of the defendant No.1 to handover collateral documents of title and after redeems the mortgage property which was mortgage to the defendant No. 3-Bank. The defendant No. 1 knows this term and without making his title perfect for sale, how he could claim the balance consideration amount within six months. The defendant No. 1 fails to deliver all the title deeds to the plaintiff that she has already adjusted its entire outstanding loan of defendant No. 3-Bank out of the money taken from the plaintiff and this fact shows that the defendant No. 1 is not ready to honour her part of the obligation. The defendant has breached the contract and thus, she cannot avoid the specific performance of contract. The fixation of time is secondary in this case and the parties have not intended the time as the essence of the contract, in as much as, obtaining the necessary deed of redemption from the defendant No. 3-bank is a condition precedent to the conferment of the perfect ownership upon the plaintiff.

29. From the above discussion, it is clear that the agreement between the parties is still subsisting despite its recission by the defendant No. 1 and that the defendant No. 1 was in error in treating it rescinded. A wrongful repudiation by one party cannot except by the election of the other party to treat it, put an end to an obligation, if the other party still insists on performance of the contract, that is to say, the parties are left with their rights and liabilities as before. What's more we can infer from the facts that the plaintiff company is willing and ready to perform it part of promise and therefore, the plaintiff is legally entitled to a decree for specific performance.

30. In this appeal another important issue is to be determined since the trial court dismissed the suit on the findings that the suit land is mortgaged to the defendant No. 3-Bank, thus execution of the Bainanama (Exhibit-2) and deed of agreement (Exhibit-3) is void as per section 53D of the Transfer of Property Act which provides: "Section 53D—Immovable Property under mortgage not to be transferred—No immovable property under registered mortgage shall be re-mortgaged or sold without the written consent of the mortgagee, and any re-mortgage or sale made otherwise shall be void".

31. The aforesaid provisions contemplates that the word "Sale" appears in that section means transfer of ownership does not impose any bar in entering into an "agreement for sale" in respect of such a land as precisely has happened in the present case to repay the loan amount and then the Deed of Sale would be executed and registered. Moreso, such an agreement for sale in respect of the suit land executed between the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 is not void as the "Deed of Agreement for Sale" (বায়নানামা দলিল) (Exhibit-2) is not the "Deed of Sale" or "Deed of Transfer" as provided under section 53D of the Transfer of Property Act. This view of ours finds support from the decision in the case of SM Hossain vs Abdul Malek reported in 1985 BLD 590. That section 53D was introduced by way of amendment for protecting the mortgagee Bank for realization loan given by it. In the instant suit the mortgagee Bank was impleaded as defendant No. 3 and requested to take the loan amount from the deposited balance amount of Taka 1,52,31,200 in court by challan No. 10233 dated 24-2-2009 on the date of filing of the suit on 24-2-2009. But the defendant No. 3 without withdrawing the arrear loan amount from the said deposited Taka 1,52,31,200 rather by filing written statement claimed that the said loan was defaulted and turned to Taka 2,35,51,370.20 with interest as on 31-12-2009 and further stated that another overdraft loan taken by defendant No. 2, husband of defendant No. 1, the said loan has now stood at Taka 68,26,000 as on 31-12-2009. So, the defendant No. 3 is now entitled Taka 2,35,51,987.20 + 68,26,000 = Total 3,03,77,987.20 with interest till adjustment of the loan liabilities or when the defendant No. 3 redeemed the mortgage in future.

32. Thus the learned Joint District Judge totally misconceived the section 53D of the Transfer of Property Act and illegally dismissed the suit.

33. Now a question may arise whether the mortgagee Bank-defendant No. 3 is entitled to Taka 3,03,77,987.20 as claimed in its written statement. Learned Advocate for the plaintiff by referring section 47 Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 argued that there is limitation of imposing claim and the Bank in no circumstance can claim interest more than 3 times of its principal loan amount i.e. Taka 22,00,000 x 3 = 66,00,000 and another over draft loan of defendant No-2 which now stood at Taka 68,26,000 with interest as on 31-12-2009. Thus the mortgagee-Bank is entitled to claim at best (Taka 66,00,000 + 68,26,000) = 1,34,26,000 not Taka 3,03,77,987.20 and same can easily adjustable from the deposited amount of Taka 1,52,31,200 deposited at the time of filing present suit on 24-2-2009. Although the payment of loan to defendant No. 3 is a matter in between the defendant No. 1 and defendant No. 3 but since the excessive claim is illegal and barred under section 47 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 and ultimately it will affect the plaintiff in obtaining Sale Deed through the process of court. Furthermore, it appears from the record that till now the defendant No. 3-Bank had not filed any suit or taken any step for realization of the loan as per section 46 of Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 which is barred under the said section. Thus there is no bar in decreeing the suit for specific performance either directing the defendant No. 3-the mortgagee Bank to redeem the mortgage of the suit land after receiving its due arrear loan from the balance deposit amount lying in the court.

34. Chapter IV of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 deals with "Of Mortgages of Immoveable Property and Charges". Section 60 of the Transfer of Property Act speaks about Rights and Liabilities of Mortgagor which conferred on the mortgagor the right to redemption mortgaged property on payment of mortgage money till right to foreclosure is exercised by the mortgagee as provided under section 67 of the Transfer of Property Act. section 60A provides that—obligation to the transfer third party instead of re-transference to mortgagor- where mortgagor has also a right to assign the mortgage-debt and transfer the mortgaged property to such third person as the mortgagor may direct and the mortgagee shall be bound to assign and transfer accordingly in favour of the said third person. The aforesaid law connecting with redemption, obligation to transfer of debt along with mortgaged property to third party instead of re-transference to Mortgagor and right of foreclosure has not been extinguished rather will apply in the proceedings under Artha Rin Adalat AM, 2003.

35. In the case of Sekandar vs Janata Bank Ltd, 22 BLC (AD) 53. In that case it has been held —A suit for establishment of right, title and interest in respect of mortgaged property by a third party is maintainable because there is no bar either expressly or impliedly in Ain to file such suit.

36. Learned Advocate Mr Neogi tried to submit that in the present case, the plaintiff has alternative remedy by way of receiving compensation in the form of money in case of breach, the contract cannot be specifically enforced. On this point he has referred a decision reported in AIR 1943 Cal 586.

37. The law with regard to Specific Performance of Contract is, so far as this country is concerned, condified in the Specific Relief Act, 1877 and under the explanation appended to section 12 of the said Act, a presumption arises in the case of contract to transfer immovable property that its breach cannot be adequately relived by compensation in money. It is true that this presumption is rebuttable but the onus of rebutting it lies heavily on the person who seeks to avoid specific performance. One of the ways in which he can discharged this onus is by showing that the contract has itself provided an alternative method of performance, namely by payment of money. But this must be of such a nature as to show that the stipulation really is to do one of two things at the election of the party who has to do it, that is, either by performance or by payment of money and not merely by showing that the stipulation is to do one certain thing with a penalty attached to secure the performance of that very thing. In the later case, the person will not be relieved from the specific performance of the thing stipulated to be done where that thing is the transference of immovable property, for, the general rule of equity is that if a thing is agreed upon to be done, though there is a penalty annexed to secure its performance, yet the very thing itself must be done. This is the rule that has now been incorporated in section 20 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877 and it is on the basis of this section that it has been repeatedly held in cases where there are penal clause like those in the contract before us that such clauses do not debar the party who has not defaulted from enforcing specific performance as they are not in the nature of alternative stipulations.

38. The question as to whether a particular contract is in the alternative form giving an election to the party committing the breach or as to whether the contract has merely added a penalty as a deterrent against its breach is always a question of construction of the contract of the contract concerned and must consequently depend upon the language used in each case and it may be that upon the language of the contract under consideration as cited by Mr Neogi in the case reported in AIR 1943 Cal 586, Nasim Ali and Blank JJ, took the view that they did take but it does not appear that in doing so they either considered section 20 of the Specific Relief Act or examined the language of the relevant contract before them with a view to ascertaining whether it provided a mere penalty or an alternative method of performance. The case does not appear to have been presented before them from this aspect.

39. Chapter 11 of the Specific Relief Act has dealt with "Of the Specific Performance for Contracts". Section 12 of the Act has dealt with the contracts which may in the discretion of the court be enforced in the discretion of the court except as otherwise provided in the Chapter. In the context, we are concerned with clause (a) and the main section it is clear that when the act agreed to be done is in the performance wholly or partly, of a trust that can be specifically enforced. In the present case, defendant No. 1, the land owner having agreed in unequivocal term to sign Bainanama and Agreement, the Specific Relief Act can very much be enforced against her within the meaning of section 27 of the Specific Relief Act. It may be stated that breach of agreement to sell the suit land cannot be adequately compensated by money as explained by the legislature in the explanation appended to the section and therefore clause (b) (c) and (d) to section 12 are also attracted in the present case. A reference may be placed in the decision of our apex court reported in 18 BLC (AD) 273.

40. We have already shown above that the plaintiff has able to established without any manner of doubt a genuine and straight forward contract was entered into between the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 on 10-4-2008 on the basis of written Bainanama Dalil executed by defendant No. 1 as well as Deed of Agreement executed by defendant Nos. 1 and 2 both the Deed was executed on 10-4-2008 and that contract was obtained from the defendant No.1 within the meaning of section 28 of the Specific Relief Act by any fraud, undue advantage, misrepresentation, concealment, unfair practice, influence or mistake of fact, misapprehension or surprise or that the stipulated price was in any way grossly inadequate with reference to the state of things existing at the date of contract. Explanation to section 12 of the Specific Relief Act specifically provides that unless and until the contrary is proved, the court shall presume that the breach of a contract to transfer immovable property cannot be adequately relieved by compensation in money. Illustration to clause (c) of section 12 of the said Act is as follows: "A contracts with B to sell him a house for Taka 1,000. B is entitled to a decree directing A to convey the house to him, he paying the purchase money".

<u>41. Section 19 of the Specific Relief Act empowers the court to award compensation for breach of contract in certain cases to the person suing for the specific performance of contract whether in addition to, or in substitution for, such performance, but in the present case nothing has been appeared.</u>

42. In the present case we have good and reliable evidence on record that defendant No. 1-vendor as ordinary women with her eyes open agreed to sell the property by duly executing a registered Bainanama Dalil at a total price of Taka 1,15,00,000 without being influenced by fraud, misrepresentation, mistake of fact etc. There is also no reason to hold that the stipulated price was in any way grossly inadequate with reference to the state of things existing at the date of contract. As defendant No.1 did not execute the kabala as per agreement, and after due service of notice on the defendant No. 1, plaintiff instituted the present suit. In the present case the plaintiff was successfully proved its continuous readiness and willingness from the date of the contract to the time of hearing of the suit to perform the contract on its part.

43. The learned Advocate for the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 further submits that the plaintiff did not take any step for registration as per terms of Bainanama within 6 months from the execution of Baina dated 10-4-2008 but plaintiff did not take any step for registration as per Baina as time prescribed for registration as per section 54A of Transfer of Property Act is 6 (six) month. But the plaintiff failed to perform its part within 6 month time, consequently defendant Nos. 1 and 2 faced financial hardship and loss. But it was stipulated in the Bainanama that no specific time was fixed for performance of the Bainanama. Rather it was stipulated in clause 5 of the Baina that defendant No. 1 and 2 will pay the entire loan liabilities including interest of the Bank within 2 month from their own source and at their responsibility and redeem the schedule property and obtained those deeds and furnished original title deeds and document to the plaintiff company. Thus it is evident that the condition of performance of the contract is not absolute rather is dependent on the performance of the promisor-vendor. If the vendor has not performed his part of the contract he/she cannot bound the promisee-vendee-plaintiff company to perform its part of the contract and the contract in such case will remain enforceable as per section 51, 52, 53 and 54 of the Contract Act, 1872. Thus the time in a contract for sale of immovable Property is not the essence of the contract. Reliance may be placed in the case reported in 17 DLR (SC) 481/ 5 BLC (AD) 119, 19 DLR 791.

<u>44. Article 113 of the Limitation Act fixed 1 year time to file a suit for Specific Performance of Contract from the date fixed for performance of the contract if no such date is fixed then from the date of refusal of performance as amended on 1-7-2005. The present suit was filed on 24-2-2009 after 10 month, 15 days from the date of Baina dated 10-4-2008 (Exhibit-2). So, the suit was filed within the period of limitation. If any conflict arose in between the time limit stated in the instrument and the relevant law, then law will prevail.</u>

45. It appears that the plaintiff filed the suit Specific Performance of Contract in pursuance of registered “বায়নানামা দলিল” dated 10-4-2008 (Exhibit- 2) and executed another unregistered “চুক্তিপত্র দলিল” dated 10-4-2008 (Exhibit-3) for removing encumbrances of the mortgage in respect of the suit land by the defendant No. 1 from Bank-defendant No. 3 which need not registered. Since the plaintiff filed the present suit for Specific Performance enforcing registered  বায়নানামা দলিল (Agreement for Sale) dated 10-4-2008 (Exhibit-2), as such there is no impediment to pass a decree for Specific Performance of Contract. Thus the argument made by the learned Advocate for defendant No. 1 and 2 that plaintiff sought Specific Performance of Contract for unregistered agreement and registered Baina deserve no merit.

46. Mr Probir Neogi has referred to the decision in the case of Abdur Razzaque Mollah vs Md Qayum Mollah, 53 DLR 535. In this reported Case for specific performance of contract, the plaintiff entered into a Bainanama within defendant No. 1 on 7-6-1986 for sale of suit properties since the defendant No. 1 failed to execute and register Sale Deed, the plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 52 of 1992 for suit properties which was mortgaged before hand to defendant No. 3, Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation against Loan Case No. Bag 8 of 1985 for loan of Taka 2,00,000 for construction house on the suit land within the knowledge of the plaintiff and the Mortgagee having obtained decree in Artha Rin Adalat Suit No. 5 of 1991 in the Court of Sub-ordinate Judge-cum-Artha Rin Adalat, Bagerhat, the instant suit for Specific Performance of Contract over the self same properties is not maintainable in law.

47. In the reported case defendant No. 1 denied the allegations of the plaintiff and contended that he never executed bainanama and the plaintiff by way of fraud and forgery created the same. He also denied the receipt of the consideration money of the so-called bainanama or handed over any possession of the suit property with intent to sell to the plaintiff.

48. Hence the facts and circumstances of the cited case are totally distinguishable from those of the present case. In the present case Bainanama and Deed of Agreement (Exhibit-2 and 3) both dated 10-4-2008 are admitted by both the plaintiff and defendant Nos. 1 and 2. Defendant No. 3-Bank also admitted that schedule 'ka' and 'kha' of the suit land was mortgaged by defendant No. 1 against the loan taken by defendant No. 2. Defendant No. 3-Bank in their written statement or in the evidence did not disclose about passing of any decree in respect of the suit mortgage land.

49. Mr Neogi has referred to another decision in the case of Monfar Raja Chowdhury vs Dewan Rawsan Kumar Khatun Chowdhury, AIR (30) 1943 Calcutta 586. But the facts of circumstances of the cited case is quite distinguishable from those of the case in hand and have no manner of application in the present case.

50. Mr AM Masum, the Learned Advocate for the Respondent No. 3 Bank seriously contended that no suit can be filed in any court challenging the decree passed by the Artha Rin Adalat. We have carefully considered this argument. But it appears from the record of the present suit, defendant no 3 Bank except filing of written statement, no document or oral evidence was adduced to prove its case. Further, the defendant No. 3 neither disclosed in its written statement that defendant No. 3 filed any Artha Rin Suit against the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 for realisation of outstanding loan amount from the said defendants or obtained any decree from court. Hence, we find no merit in such submission of the learned Advocate. Learned Advocate further placed reliance in the decisions reported in 57 DLR (AD) 64 and 63 DLR (AD) 326. It fail to understand why learned Advocate, Mr Masum has cited those cases. The facts and the principles of law applicable in those cases are quite distinguishable in the present case.

51. In the result, the appeal is allowed. It is ordered that the suit is decreed on contest against the defendant Nos. 1-3. The plaintiff shall get the saf kabala deed executed by the defendant No.1 by receiving the balance consideration money of Taka 18,05,200 (Taka eighteen lac, five thousand and two hundred) only to the defendant No.1 and defendant No. 1 is directed to pay outstanding loan liabilities of defendant No. 3-Bank out of the deposited amount of Taka 1,52,31,200 after redeeming the mortgage property described in the schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha' to the plaint within a period of three months from the date of receipt of the record by the Joint District Judge, Seventh Court, Dhaka and Defendant No.1 is directed to execute and register the kabala in respect of the suit land in favour of the plaintiff-company whereupon the defendant No. 1 shall execute and register the necessary kabala/kabalas. If the defendant No. 1 after redeeming the suit mortgage lands fails to execute and register necessary kabala on receipt of the said balance consideration money, the plaintiff shall get the kabala executed and registered through court by receiving the balance consideration money of Taka 18,05,200 (Taka eighteen lac, five thousand and two hundred) only and also directed the defendant No. 3 bank to receive their outstanding loan liabilities money amounting to Taka 1,34,26,000 from the deposited amount of Taka 1,52,31,200 now lying in court after redeeming the mortgage of the suit land.

52. There is no order as to costs.

Let the records be sent down along with a copy of this judgment to the trial court as early as possible.

End.
